title: Are Young Indians Actually Choosing to Stay Single?
meta_title: Are Young Indians Actually Choosing to Stay Single? | Aperture
summary: 42% of Indians above 26 say they don't want to marry. But Deloitte's 2026 data shows finances are the bigger driver. Here's what the numbers say.
primary_question: Are young Indians choosing to stay single, or just priced out of marriage?

content:
For some young Indians, staying single is a genuine choice. For many more, it's a financial reality dressed up as one. About 42% of Indians above 26 say they don't want to get married, according to a 2025 survey. But Deloitte's 2026 India report found something telling alongside that: 54% of Gen Zs had delayed a major life decision because of financial pressure. Marriage usually tops that list. These two numbers are not describing the same people.

Key Takeaways

  • About 42% of Indians above 26 say they don't want to marry, but this number skews toward urban, educated groups
  • Deloitte's 2026 India survey found 54% of Gen Zs delayed major life decisions due to financial strain, including marriage
  • India's Total Fertility Rate has dropped to 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1
  • The average marriage age for urban Indian women has risen to 27, a significant shift from earlier generations
  • "Choosing single" and "financially delaying" are two separate categories that most headlines treat as the same thing

Is Staying Single Actually a Choice?

For some, absolutely. For a lot of others, not really. According to Deloitte's 2026 India Gen Z and Millennial Survey, 54% of Gen Zs delayed major life decisions due to financial pressure. A separate Statista finding shows 23% of Indian Gen Z want neither marriage nor children. That's a deliberate preference. The others are a different story.

The honest version: two distinct groups show up in these surveys. One is genuinely opting out. The other wants stability first and hasn't quite found it yet. Treating them as the same trend misses most of what's actually happening.

What the Numbers Actually Show

Something interesting has begun to show in India's marriage statistics over the past two decades. The average age at first marriage for urban Indian women is now 27. India's Total Fertility Rate stands at 1.9, below the 2.1 needed for population replacement. And a 2025 survey found 42% of Indians above 26 saying they're not interested in marriage at all.

Context matters, though. The 42% figure skews heavily toward urban and educated respondents. The national picture is different. Rural marriage patterns remain closer to what they've always been, though the age is creeping upward there too.

Two Groups the Data Keeps Conflating

FactorActively Choosing SingleFinancially Delaying
Primary driverValues, independence, identityHousing cost, wedding expense, job uncertainty
View on marriage"Not for me""When the time is right"
Approximate share of Gen ZAbout 23%Likely 30% or more
Typical profileUrban, highly educated, often earning wellBroader, includes semi-urban graduates
Social pressure responseComfortable saying noStill managing family expectations

On the surface, these two groups look identical from outside. But they're drawing on definately different motivations, and conversations that treat them as one trend tend to answer the wrong question.

Why Is Affording Marriage So Difficult Now?

The cost problem is real. A modest Indian wedding runs anywhere from 3 to 15 lakhs. A 2 BHK apartment in Bengaluru or Pune costs upwards of 80 lakhs. And 60% of Gen Zs in India told Deloitte in 2026 that housing affordability directly shapes their major life choices. This isn't a fringe concern.

On top of that, 20% of Indian Gen Zs say they struggle to cover living expenses monthly. When you're not sure about rent, committing to a wedding and a shared home feels impossible. But that's not the same thing as choosing to stay single. Most of this group hasn't decided. They're waiting untill the maths improves. For more on how Indian Gen Z is spending right now, see our piece on doom spending among young Indians.

Does Being Single Make Financial Sense in India?

Sort of. India doesn't allow joint filing for income tax, so there's no direct marriage bonus the way some countries have. Single people tend to spend less in the short term and carry fewer shared obligations. But they're also building household assets slower, often renting longer, and absorbing risk without a second income.

The one genuinely cheaper thing: not having a wedding. A 5 to 10 lakh saving over skipping the ceremony goes a long way toward a down payment. Whether that's a feature or a side effect depends entirely on the person.

What Families and Society Actually Think

It depends on where you are. In metro cities and among urban professionals, being single in your late 20s is increasingly unremarkable. At most workplaces in Bengaluru or Mumbai, nobody particularly cares. In smaller cities and towns, the pressure to marry by 27 or 28 is still intense and doesn't ease until much later.

The gap between what young people want and what their families expect is widening faster than the conversation around it is. That friction accounts for a lot of the anxiety the surveys keep finding, more than the question of marriage itself. Frequently Asked Questions

Are young Indians actually choosing to stay single?

Some are. About 23% of Indian Gen Z say they want neither marriage nor children, according to Statista. But a larger portion, 54% by Deloitte's 2026 India count, has delayed major life decisions due to financial strain. Choosing single and being priced out of settling down look similar from outside but come from very different places.

Is India's marriage rate actually declining?

Yes, measurably. India's Total Fertility Rate fell to 1.9, below the 2.1 replacement level. Urban marriage ages are rising, and surveys show younger groups rejecting or delaying marriage at higher rates than earlier generations. The trend is real in cities and among educated 20-somethings, even if the national picture is still more traditional.

Why do young Indians delay marriage for financial reasons?

Three costs dominate: wedding expenses, typically 3 to 15 lakhs even for modest ceremonies; urban housing, often 70 to 90 lakhs for a small apartment; and job instability. Deloitte's 2026 India report found 60% of Gen Zs say housing affordability shapes major life decisions. Until those numbers change, delayed marriages will stay the norm.

Is staying single becoming more socially acceptable in India?

Increasingly, yes, in urban areas. The "soft life" framing has made singlehood more visible and culturally legitimate among educated young Indians. But nationally, marriage remains nearly universal. In smaller cities, family pressure still kicks in hard by the late 20s. The urban and rural experiences are quite different.

What does the Deloitte 2026 India survey say about Gen Z and marriage?

The Deloitte 2026 India Gen Z and Millennial Survey found 54% of Indian Gen Zs delayed major life decisions, including marriage, due to financial pressure. It also found 60% say housing affordability affects their life choices, and 20% struggle to cover living expenses monthly. These figures complicate the simple "choosing single" narrative considerably.

The Short Version

India's Gen Z isn't one group. Some genuinely don't want to marry, and that 23% figure reflects a real and growing preference. But the bigger story is financial: 54% of Indian Gen Zs have delayed major life decisions because of money, and marriage is usually on that list. Most headlines treat these as one trend. They're not. The marriage rate is declining, and the honest answer is that India's single population is growing partly by choice and partly because housing and wedding costs make settling down feel impossibly out of reach for a lot of people right now.
